problem.title: Retail demand forecasting
problem.context: A retailer forecasts weekly demand per store and product: 400 stores and 30,000 products. Every Monday the forecasts for the next eight weeks feed the replenishment system, which orders stock. Sales from the tills reach the company's data warehouse every night; promotions and public holidays move demand strongly. A team of three data scientists owns the forecasting pipeline end to end. The data warehouse is run by the central IT department, which the team cannot change.

requirements.text: Produce, every week, the forecast per store and product for the next eight weeks, and deliver it to the replenishment system by Monday 06:00.
Run the forecast again for any past week exactly as it was produced.
Try new model ideas and compare them with the production model on past weeks before they replace it.
Asked for the forecast of a week up to two years back, the team produces the same numbers within one working day.
A new model idea that beats the production model on past weeks reaches production within one week, with no manual step except the approval.
When a weekly run fails, the team is told within 15 minutes, and the replenishment system never receives a partial forecast.
A new team member can run the whole pipeline on their own machine within their first week.
Three data scientists, with no data engineers; the data warehouse stays as it is.
The weekly run must fit in the six hours between the nightly load and the Monday deadline.

points.description: The system queries source systems into a managed, orchestrated ML pipeline that prepares data, trains and compares candidate models by a selected metric, and versions pipelines, artifacts, and experiments together. Repository commits trigger staged testing and deployment, including repeated full-pipeline integration tests, while scheduled batch scoring writes predictions to storage and automatically recovers from operational failures. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, repeatable releases, and resilient batch operations, but sacrifices prediction freshness compared with online serving. It also emphasizes failure recovery rather than detecting model-quality or data-drift degradation, and managed orchestration and full-pipeline tests add operational cost.

An orchestrated, repeatable ML pipeline on a standalone managed cloud ML service batch-extracts and transforms row-level features, trains and tunes models, evaluates candidates offline against held-out truth, and selects them for deployment. Immutable, provenance-preserving data and end-to-end versioning govern datasets, snapshots, experiments, artifacts, health, and pipeline dependencies; automated full-pipeline integration tests and release automation deploy or restore versions, while predictions are precomputed for later serving. Trade-off: This favors reproducibility, auditability, regression detection, recovery, and predictable batch serving. It gives up freshness and low-latency responsiveness, while batch processing, full-pipeline testing, and preserved versions increase delay and compute/storage costs; manual recovery intervention reduces release autonomy.

The system pulls source records by query, then practitioners develop understandable model code in Jupyter and an IDE and manually run preparation, training, validation, and deployment on a managed cloud ML platform. It preserves a held-out test set, versions deployable artifacts and dependencies, and schedules batch scoring with results written to storage or analytics systems. Trade-off: This gains a relatively simple, reproducible path to governed batch deployment and protects evaluation from data snooping. It gives up automated orchestration, rapid adaptation, continuously fresh or online predictions, and consistent dependency governance across development environments.

Source data is pulled by query into an orchestrated, repeatable ML pipeline whose stages can use managed services or pluggable engines. It trains candidate algorithms/configurations in parallel, selects them by validation metrics, records lifecycle traceability, validates data and models automatically, releases changes progressively with rollback, and serves scheduled batch predictions; new production or labeled data drives retraining. Trade-off: This gains repeatable experimentation, governed lineage, safer releases, and less manual maintenance. It gives up online prediction immediacy and incurs complexity and compute costs from hybrid execution, parallel training, validation, and automated retraining.

Query-based extraction pulls source records into an immutable, provenance-preserving store, where managed, orchestrated pipelines prepare data, train and compare candidates, and version definitions, artifacts, and experiments together. Commits trigger staged builds and releases, with full-pipeline integration tests; the selected model is deployed for scheduled batch scoring, while service, data-quality, and performance monitoring tracks production behavior. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, governance, and automated control, but batch delivery sacrifices prediction freshness and immediate responsiveness. Immutable retention, repeated full-pipeline tests, and managed services add storage, compute, and operational cost.

External sources are batch-extracted, transformed, and loaded as row-level features, with provenance and immutable preservation, into an orchestrated pipeline on a standalone managed cloud ML platform. The pipeline trains and evaluates candidates offline, governs datasets, experiments, artifacts, and model health end to end, runs full-pipeline integration tests, and promotes releases through progressively gated environments before generating periodic predictions for serving. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, traceability, repeatable validation, and controlled promotion, but gives up prediction freshness and responsiveness because ingestion and serving are batch-based. It also incurs substantial orchestration, testing, governance, and release overhead.

Source records are queried into a managed, orchestrated ML pipeline that validates data, runs parallel candidate training, selects candidates by a performance metric, and records lifecycle metadata. Approved releases are progressively deployed with rollback, while scheduled batch scoring writes predictions to storage or analytics systems and monitoring of service health, dependencies, data quality, and shifts informs adaptation. Trade-off: This gains repeatability, comparison, governance, safer releases, and operational visibility, but increases compute and coordination costs. Query-based ingestion and scheduled batch serving also limit prediction freshness and depend on extraction schedules and downstream storage.

CDC delivers source changes into an orchestrated, repeatable managed-cloud ML pipeline that versions definitions, artifacts, and experiments, trains and compares candidates by a selected metric, and validates the full pipeline. Environment-gated automation promotes approved releases to scheduled batch scoring, while results are stored for downstream use and service, dependency, data-quality, shift, and performance signals are monitored. Trade-off: This favors reproducibility, controlled promotion, and broad operational visibility, but predictions are only as fresh as the batch schedule rather than real time. Full-pipeline testing, version governance, and managed execution add runtime, infrastructure, and operational overhead.

Source records are queried with provenance and immutable preservation, then passed through a repeatable, orchestrated managed pipeline whose definitions, experiments, and artifacts are versioned together. The system compares candidate models by validation metric, runs full-pipeline integration tests, and uses environment-gated automation to deploy scheduled batch scoring while monitoring service health, data quality, shifts, and model performance. Trade-off: This favors reproducibility, auditability, controlled promotion, and operational visibility, but query extraction and immutable retention add overhead, while batch serving sacrifices freshness and interactive latency. Metric-driven selection and approval gates may also slow releases or overemphasize the chosen metric.

Batch ETL loads traceable, preserved row-level features into an orchestrated managed-cloud ML pipeline for preparation, training, tuning, offline evaluation, and deployment. Versioned datasets, artifacts, experiments, metadata, and model health support reproducibility, while explicitly declared production dependencies, full-pipeline integration tests, and environment-gated automation control releases. Trade-off: This gains auditability, repeatability, and safer promotion, but batch ingestion, offline evaluation, and precomputed serving reduce data freshness and responsiveness. Comprehensive lifecycle governance and repeated full-pipeline testing improve confidence but add storage, execution, and operational overhead.

The system queries source systems into a managed, orchestrated pipeline that validates data, prepares features, trains vertically scalable models, compares candidates by metric, and records comprehensive lifecycle metadata. Validated releases are deployed progressively for scheduled batch scoring, with results stored for analytics and service, data-quality, and model monitoring guiding adaptation. Trade-off: This gains repeatability, traceability, automated safeguards, and rollback while simplifying batch operations. It gives up low-latency freshness and horizontal training scalability, and query extraction may increase source-system load and pipeline latency.

Change-data-capture events feed an orchestrated, managed-cloud ML pipeline whose definitions, experiments, and artifacts are versioned together. The pipeline tests the full workflow, compares candidates by selected metrics, promotes releases through environment-specific gates, and schedules batch predictions while monitoring service health, data quality, and shifts using explicitly reproducible production dependencies. Trade-off: This gains repeatability, auditability, and controlled promotion with operational visibility, but gives up low-latency predictions and may incur substantial orchestration, testing, monitoring, and managed-platform costs. Batch freshness is limited by the scoring schedule.

approaches.idea: What if managed orchestration and automatic recovery provide the weekly operational backbone?
What if exact historical reconstruction and auditability dominate the design?
What if a small team keeps the workflow manual and the managed platform handles only infrastructure?
approaches.dropped_because: Manual script-driven transitions cannot credibly satisfy the one-week model release and six-hour weekly operating constraints without adding the automation this approach avoids.

approaches.idea: What if broad hybrid execution, parallel training, retraining, and rollback maximize adaptability?
What if a standalone managed service and change capture minimize custom integration while retaining automated comparison and monitoring?

trajectory.hypothesis: Managed orchestration, staged release, and automatic recovery should reduce manual operations for the small team and support R1, R3, Q2, and Q3; batch serving should fit R1.

tradeoffs.note: Scheduled batch delivery fits periodic replenishment with limited serving machinery, but this value alone does not guarantee atomic publication or a 15-minute alert.

trajectory.observation: The point provides a coherent automation path, but failure recovery is not the same as observing data quality or model shifts. The combination has no attesting source; the exact delivery SLA and run duration remain unproven.

trajectory.hypothesis: Immutable data, complete lifecycle governance, and offline held-out evaluation should best support R2, R3, and Q1; managed cloud infrastructure limits specialist operations.

tradeoffs.note: Retaining immutable inputs and lifecycle snapshots supports historical reconstruction, but storage and repeated offline processing have no measured six-hour bound.

trajectory.observation: This is the strongest historical audit path so far. Manual intervention during recovery and batch ingestion/serving leave the one-week release and run-time targets unproven; no source attests the full combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: A managed platform, readable code, and declared dependencies should ease onboarding and local execution for Q4 while avoiding a bespoke platform for C1.

tradeoffs.note: Manual script transitions reduce platform work but make repeatable comparison and a fast approved release dependent on people.

trajectory.observation: The point protects a held-out test set and uses understandable code, but manual orchestration directly conflicts with rapid promotion and leaves the weekly cadence fragile. The approach was dropped after this seed.

trajectory.hypothesis: Hybrid engines, parallel candidate training, automatic retraining, and rollback should favor Q2, R3, and the weekly throughput target C2.

tradeoffs.note: Hybrid engines and parallel work offer adaptable experimentation but increase integration and operational load for three data scientists and lack evidence of meeting the run window.

trajectory.observation: The combination is highly automated but more complex than the team's staffing constraint supports. Batch delivery still suits replenishment, while the asserted runtime benefit of parallel work is not benchmarked. No source attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add preserved, traceable input data and replace recovery-only monitoring with service and data-quality monitoring to improve R2, Q1, and Q3.

tradeoffs.note: Immutable preservation improves replayability but adds storage and does not establish the six-hour processing bound.

trajectory.observation: The revised point adds provenance and broader operational signals while preserving the automated comparison and batch path. Monitoring supports rapid visibility but does not specify alert timing or atomic output delivery. No source attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace manual recovery intervention with environment-gated automated promotion to improve Q2 while retaining the strong historical evidence for R2 and Q1.

tradeoffs.note: Automated gated promotion reduces manual release work, while environment gates alone do not ensure failed forecasts are withheld or alert within 15 minutes.

trajectory.observation: The point improves release automation without weakening offline evaluation or traceability, though the full lifecycle governance and testing overhead remains unmeasured. No source attests the full combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Move from hybrid infrastructure to managed pipeline-centered infrastructure and replace automatic retraining with monitoring, retaining candidate parallelism and rollback while reducing C1 risk.

tradeoffs.note: Managed orchestration reduces platform ownership and parallel candidates aid comparison, but concurrency and broader lifecycle work still have unverified run-time cost.

trajectory.observation: The managed infrastructure reduces one major complexity source and broader monitoring is more useful for failure visibility. Parallel candidate work and continuous retraining remain costly risks for the small team. No source attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Use a standalone managed ML service with change-data capture, gated release, metric comparison, and monitoring to explore an automated path with less platform composition than A or D.

tradeoffs.note: Change capture and managed automation can reduce custom integration, but the warehouse is centrally operated and neither access nor end-to-end batch runtime is specified.

trajectory.observation: This gives a distinct standalone-service route with operational coverage, but change capture may require central IT changes and is a poor fit unless the existing warehouse already exposes it. No source attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace commit-triggered release with environment-gated promotion while keeping preserved data, metric comparison, testing, and monitoring; this should better fit approval-only release governance for Q2.

tradeoffs.note: Environment gates provide a controlled approval point, but they do not define atomic forecast publishing or time-bounded failure alerts.

trajectory.observation: This is A's best point: immutable inputs and lifecycle versioning improve historical replay, while monitoring and full-pipeline tests broaden the reliability controls. Q1's one-day target, Q2's one-week target, Q3's alert and atomicity targets, and the run-time constraint still need operational verification. No source attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Declare production dependencies explicitly to improve Q4 while retaining B's immutable data, complete lifecycle versioning, offline evaluation, and gated release.

tradeoffs.note: Versioned datasets, artifacts, and explicit runtimes support reconstructing an old run and setting up a local environment, but the comprehensive governance and tests need a measured runtime budget.

trajectory.observation: This is B's best point and the strongest local-environment specification in the search. Its offline scoring path is predictable, but it does not prove it can finish inside the six-hour window. No source attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace parallel candidate training with vertically scalable training to reduce coordination and compute overhead for C1 and C2 while preserving validation, lifecycle traceability, rollback, and monitoring.

tradeoffs.note: A larger single machine may reduce distributed coordination for a small team, but it limits parallel candidate throughput and is not benchmarked against the required workload.

trajectory.observation: This is D's best point. It removes hybrid infrastructure and concurrent training overhead, but six-hour feasibility remains an assumption and automated retraining remains operationally broad. No source attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add explicitly specified production dependencies to E's automated managed service path to improve independent local setup for Q4.

tradeoffs.note: Automated change ingestion and declared runtimes support repeatability, but using CDC may require central-IT cooperation that the constraint does not grant.

trajectory.observation: This is E's best point. Explicit dependencies improve portability, but the warehouse constraint makes CDC an approximate and conditional fit. The candidate remains distinct from pipeline-centered infrastructure and no source attests the complete combination.

alternatives.name: Managed, monitored weekly batch pipeline
alternatives.summary: Use query extraction into managed orchestration, version experiments and preserve source inputs, gate releases, run full-pipeline checks, and monitor data and service health before scheduled batch delivery.

choices.reason: Pulls from the existing warehouse without requiring it to be replaced; query permissions and runtime remain to be confirmed.

Repeatable connected stages support weekly runs and candidate evaluation. Productionizing Machine Learning with a Microservices Architecture and MLOps: Model management, deployment, and monitoring with Azure Machine Learning describe orchestrated pipelines.
Managed pipeline infrastructure limits platform operation for a team without data engineers; MLOps: Model management, deployment, and monitoring with Azure Machine Learning describes this approach.
Compares multiple candidate models on validation metrics before promotion.
Versions pipeline definitions, artifacts, and experiments together for comparison and replay.
Gated automated promotion preserves the requested approval while automating other release stages.
Scheduled batch output matches the weekly replenishment interface; atomic publication still needs implementation detail.
Service and data-quality signals provide the right monitoring coverage, though no 15-minute alert guarantee is specified.
Repeated whole-pipeline validation can catch integration failures before production delivery.
Preserved provenance and immutable inputs help reconstruct historical forecasts.

considered.reason: The seed used automated recovery, but service and data-quality monitoring gives better failure visibility.

open.reason: The six-hour capacity depends on concrete hardware, workload, and runtime measurements not settled by this alternative.

relations.note: The design chooses the required ingestion mechanism before the orchestrated workflow.
The design chooses workflow coordination along with model evaluation.

alternatives.summary: Use batch ETL, offline held-out evaluation, immutable data, end-to-end lifecycle governance, explicit production dependencies, and gated managed-cloud delivery.

choices.reason: ETL is aligned with nightly warehouse data and keeps the warehouse as the source.
Repeatable orchestration supports scheduled forecasts and retrospective candidate evaluation.
A standalone managed platform avoids a team-owned execution stack and offers a reproducible runtime.
Offline comparison against held-out truth supports historical model selection.
End-to-end governance includes training snapshots, dataset versions, experiments, and artifacts.
Immutable provenance-preserving data supports the input side of exact replay.
Precomputed offline forecasts match the weekly batch consumption pattern.
Environment gates automate promotion while retaining an approval boundary.
Full-pipeline integration checks validate the combined offline workflow before release.
Declared production dependencies make the production environment easier to reproduce locally.

considered.reason: Recovery can allow manual intervention, which is weaker for the approval-only release target.

open.reason: The alternative does not select or benchmark a concrete runtime resource strategy against six hours.

relations.note: The required ETL ingestion choice is included.
The required workflow coordination choice is included.

alternatives.name: Managed, traceable pipeline with rollback
alternatives.summary: Keep managed pipeline infrastructure, lifecycle traceability, metric comparison, service and data monitoring, and progressive rollback, while choosing vertical training to limit distributed coordination.

choices.reason: Query extraction works with an unchanged warehouse if access is available.
An orchestrated workflow supports repeated runs and candidate comparisons.
Managed pipeline-centered infrastructure reduces team-owned operations.
Vertical scaling avoids distributed training coordination for a small team; its capacity remains unmeasured.
Metric-driven candidate evaluation supports comparison before release.
Comprehensive traceability links datasets, runs, artifacts, and model health.
Progressive deployment with rollback reduces the impact of a problematic model release.
Scheduled batch scoring fits replenishment's weekly handoff; all-or-nothing publication is still open.
Service and data-quality monitoring improves operational visibility.
Automated data and model validation protects retraining and deployment transitions.

considered.reason: The seed's hybrid engines add complexity inconsistent with the small team.
Parallel candidates may speed comparison but add coordination and unmeasured compute cost.

open.reason: Vertical training is only a strategy; no workload benchmark proves the six-hour target.

relations.note: Query extraction is selected alongside orchestration.
Workflow coordination is included as required by model evaluation.

alternatives.name: Standalone managed service with change capture
alternatives.summary: Use a standalone managed cloud service, automated pipeline and gated promotion, with change capture, full-pipeline checks, monitoring, and explicit production dependencies.

choices.reason: Change capture can reduce delay between the nightly source load and pipeline start if central IT already exposes it; this fit is conditional.
choices.fit_note: The problem says the centrally operated warehouse is unchanged; the design space's change-capture value does not say whether this team can access or configure CDC.

choices.reason: Orchestration automates repeatable training, evaluation, and deployment stages.
A standalone managed platform limits custom platform operations for the small team.
Metric-driven candidate evaluation enables objective historical comparison.
Versioned pipelines, artifacts, and experiments preserve the comparison context.
Gated automation supports approval-led releases.
Scheduled batch prediction supplies the replenishment system on its weekly cadence.
Service and data-quality signals offer production visibility but do not themselves guarantee alert timing.
Repeated full-pipeline integration checks protect the release path.
Explicit production dependencies make a clean local setup more reproducible.

considered.reason: Query-based extraction is a safer fallback if central IT does not expose change capture.

open.reason: No runtime resource choice was checked against the six-hour workload.

relations.note: The point includes the required ingestion choice.
The point includes the workflow coordination required by evaluation.

adrs.title: Weekly data path, orchestration, and batch delivery
adrs.context: Nightly warehouse data must feed a weekly eight-week forecast without changing the centrally operated warehouse. The small team needs a repeatable batch path, while the design space does not specify the retailer's interface contract or measured run capacity.

options.name: Managed pipeline and query extraction
pros: Keeps the warehouse as an external source and provides managed orchestration for scheduled forecasts.
cons: Query permissions, output atomicity, and batch runtime need implementation and measurement.
options.reason: A1 prioritizes operational monitoring and preserved input data; D1 uses the same managed batch path with lifecycle traceability and rollback.

options.name: ETL and standalone managed cloud platform
pros: Aligns with nightly batch data and limits platform ownership.
cons: Batch freshness and the required delivery time still need validation.
options.reason: B1 favors a predictable offline scoring path and low custom infrastructure.

options.name: Change capture and standalone managed cloud platform
pros: Can begin promptly after source changes while retaining a managed batch forecast path.
cons: The warehouse team may need to expose CDC, which is not guaranteed under C1.
options.reason: E1 is a conditional option when the existing warehouse already makes change capture available.

adrs.title: Historical replay and model comparison
adrs.context: Forecasts must be reconstructed for prior weeks and new model ideas must be compared against production on historical data. Immutable input data and versioned runs improve replay, but no value guarantees identical numeric output within one working day for a two-year retention period.

options.name: Metric comparison with versioned experiments and preserved data
pros: Keeps candidate comparison context and immutable source inputs for replay.
cons: The one-day reproduction target and two-year retention need operational policy and verification.
options.reason: A1 and E1 combine versioned experiments with data preservation and validation metrics.

options.name: Metric comparison with versioned experiments
pros: Preserves experiment and artifact versions for candidate comparison.
cons: Does not explicitly select immutable source preservation.
options.reason: E1 favors a compact managed-service path and relies on recorded pipeline and experiment versions.

options.name: Offline held-out evaluation with lifecycle governance
pros: Provides the broadest captured history of data, snapshots, model artifacts, and evaluation.
cons: Comprehensive governance and full-pipeline execution can add storage and compute overhead.
options.reason: B1 puts reproducibility and auditability ahead of minimizing process overhead.

options.name: Metric comparison with comprehensive traceability
pros: Connects experiment metrics to data, run, artifact, and health metadata.
cons: Does not explicitly preserve immutable raw inputs in this point.
options.reason: D1 favors lifecycle traceability while keeping a managed pipeline and rollback.

adrs.title: Promotion and production reliability controls
adrs.context: Successful model candidates should move to production within a week after approval, and failed runs must be visible without exposing partial forecasts. Automated promotion, monitoring, and integration validation address parts of this path; the design space contains no explicit 15-minute notification or atomic-output guarantee.

options.name: Environment-gated promotion with health monitoring and full-pipeline tests
pros: Automates validation and promotion across environments while monitoring service and data health.
cons: Approval-only release timing, alert latency, and all-or-nothing publication must be implemented and verified.
options.reason: The three approaches share this balance of automated release, monitoring, and integration checks.

options.name: Gated promotion with full-pipeline tests
pros: Automates release gates and validates pipeline integration.
cons: This alternative has no selected production monitoring value.
options.reason: B1 prioritizes controlled release with a comprehensive offline validation path.

options.name: Progressive rollback with monitoring and automated data/model validation
pros: Rollback and validation lower the risk of promoting a defective candidate.
cons: The point does not itself define the alert SLA or prevent partial batch visibility.
options.reason: D1 chooses stronger rollback and data/model checks to manage release risk.

adrs.title: Portable development environment
adrs.context: A new data scientist should run the pipeline locally during their first week. Managed services reduce infrastructure setup, and explicit production dependencies help reproduce runtime packages, but neither guarantees that every cloud service or credential is available locally.

options.name: Declared production dependencies
pros: Packages and runtime resources are explicitly specified for reproducible setup.
cons: Development environments are not necessarily governed by the same dependency policy; cloud access can still block a full local run.
options.reason: B1 and E1 include dependency declarations to shorten onboarding.

options.name: Managed execution without an explicit dependency choice
pros: Reduces the amount of infrastructure a new team member must operate.
cons: Does not specify the dependencies needed to run the complete pipeline on a personal machine.
options.reason: A1 and D1 reduce platform burden but leave local environment reproducibility as an implementation task.

adrs.title: Training execution shape
adrs.context: The team has no data engineers, so distributed-training coordination may add operational work. The design space distinguishes larger-machine training from parallel candidate training, but neither choice proves capacity for this forecast workload.

options.name: Vertically scalable training
cons: A single larger machine may not fit the workload and provides no measured runtime guarantee.
options.reason: D1 uses the simpler training shape to reduce coordination for the three-person team.

unaddressed.note: The search did not evaluate a runtime resource strategy or workload benchmark. No checked point establishes that 400 by 30,000 eight-week forecasts finish within six hours; benchmark the chosen model and data path before treating this constraint as met.
